section_title: The King Stands Silent before His Accusers

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 11 Meanwhile Jesus stood before the governor, who questioned Him: “Are You the King of the Jews?” “You have said so,” Jesus replied. 12 And when He was accused by the chief priests and elders, He gave no answer. 13 Then Pilate asked Him, “Do You not hear how many charges they are bringing against You?” 14 But Jesus gave no answer, not even to a single charge, much to the governor’s amazement.

context_lines: Matthew returns to Jesus standing before Pilate. The governor asks whether He is the King of the Jews, and Jesus replies that Pilate has said so. When the chief priests and elders bring accusations, He gives no answer. Pilate is amazed that He does not respond to the charges.

The question about kingship connects the hearing with the identity that has run through Matthew. His opening chapters introduced the search for the newborn King; now the governor questions a prisoner about that title. The following scenes will return to it in the crowd's choice, the soldiers' mockery, and the inscription at the cross.

[John 18:33–38](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/18.htm) gives a longer conversation about Jesus' kingdom and His witness to the truth. Jesus explains that His kingdom does not come from this world, pointing out that His servants would otherwise have fought against His arrest. Matthew focuses on His brief answer about kingship and His silence toward the accusations.
common_interpretation_lines: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus as affirming His kingship without accepting the assumptions of a rival political claimant, and His silence as a willing approach to suffering. [Wesley on 27:11](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-matthew/) stresses that His silence is not fear, while the [US Catholic bishops' notes on 27:11–14](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/matthew/27) distinguish His kingship from Pilate's expectations and connect His silence with Isaiah's suffering servant.
god_plan_lines: [Isaiah 53:7–12](https://biblehub.com/bsb/isaiah/53.htm) describes the servant's silence under oppression, His unjust treatment, and His bearing others' sins. [Acts 8:30–35](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/8.htm) explicitly uses that Scripture to explain the good news about Jesus. This is a connection the New Testament itself makes, giving His silence a place within His saving work rather than treating it merely as a refusal to cooperate.

The kingdom He describes in [John 18:36–37](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/18.htm) is bound to His witness to the truth, not to His followers fighting to prevent His death. The apparent weakness of the prisoner does not settle the truth of His claim. His way toward the cross is part of the work through which the King brings salvation.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
